name: OpenSSLNTRU (libsntrup761 + engntru OpenSSL ENGINE)
baseline: OpenSSL TLS 1.3 key exchange (ASM-optimized X25519 and P-256)
workload: Custom ~300-line tls_timer client performs 8,192 sequential TLS 1.3 handshakes between an Intel Core i7-6700 client and an AMD Ryzen 7 2700X server over Gigabit Ethernet, measuring average connections/sec; separately, cycle-counted key generation on a Haswell CPU.
claimed_speedup: sntrup761 post-quantum KEM completes more TLS 1.3 sessions/sec than OpenSSL 1.1.1k's ASM-optimized X25519 and P-256 (reported as CDF curves, not tabulated numbers); key generation takes 156317 Haswell cycles vs 269191 for the earlier CECPQ2 ntruhrss701 KEM (~1.7x faster keygen)
hardware: Client: Intel Core i7-6700; Server: AMD Ryzen 7 2700X; key-generation cycle counts measured on Haswell
tradeoffs: Requires patching OpenSSL (1.1.1f-1.1.1m only, not tested against 3.x); post-quantum-only KEM, not a general TLS library; experimental/demo-quality integration; no formal security audit of engntru/libsntrup761.
caveats: Paper (arXiv:2106.08759) is by D.J. Bernstein et al. and may have appeared in a peer-reviewed venue, but venue could not be independently confirmed this session (Semantic Scholar/DBLP fetches were blocked/rate-limited), so it is scored as a first-party claim (tier C) rather than tier B. The headline 'more handshakes/sec' result is shown only as a CDF plot in the paper, not as a single tabulated number. No LICENSE file found in the downloadable tarballs.
found_via: arXiv API search 'all:TLS AND all:OpenSSL AND all:performance' -> arXiv:2106.08759 'OpenSSLNTRU: Faster post-quantum TLS key exchange' -> https://opensslntru.cr.yp.to

name: Cloudflare ChaCha20-Poly1305 (sslconfig OpenSSL patch)
workload: TLS AEAD 'seal' operation with 13 bytes of associated data (matching TLS record framing), plaintext sizes 64-16384 bytes, cycles/byte on a Haswell CPU with AVX2.
claimed_speedup: Average 7% faster than OpenSSL 1.1.0-pre's ChaCha20-Poly1305 for short TLS records; below 2 cycles/byte for large records (exact numbers shown only as graphs, not tabulated)
hardware: Haswell CPU with AVX2 (exact model not stated)
tradeoffs: x86-64 assembly only (Sandy Bridge+/AVX2 paths); this exact code (by Vlad Krasnov / Cloudflare, with Andy Polyakov) was subsequently merged upstream into OpenSSL itself, so modern OpenSSL/BoringSSL already ship an equivalent fast ChaCha20-Poly1305 path -- the speed advantage over *current* OpenSSL is likely gone.
caveats: Numbers are read off a graph in the blog post, not tabulated; compiler and exact CPU model are not stated (tier capped at C). Historical result from 2015 comparing to a pre-release OpenSSL 1.1.0 that did not yet have this code; since the same assembly was later contributed upstream, this is mainly of historical/pedagogical interest now, not a currently-valid 'faster than OpenSSL' claim.
found_via: Blog fetch: WebFetch on Cloudflare blog post 'It takes two to ChaCha (Poly)' (blog.cloudflare.com/it-takes-two-to-chacha-poly/), found via query 'Cloudflare ChaCha20-Poly1305 TLS performance'

name: FreeBSD in-kernel TLS (kTLS) with NIC TLS offload
workload: Netflix nginx video-serving appliance streaming TLS-encrypted video at ~90 Gb/s over a single 100GbE NIC, comparing CPU utilization needed to sustain that rate with software kTLS record framing/encryption vs. Chelsio T6 NIC hardware TLS offload (both replacing plain userspace OpenSSL AES-NI + sendfile).
claimed_speedup: At the same 90Gb/s throughput: 68% CPU with software kTLS vs 35% CPU with Chelsio T6 NIC kTLS offload; software kTLS itself is motivated as retaining async sendfile(9)'s advantages (fewer context switches, no extra memory copy) that plain userspace OpenSSL + sendfile cannot get because OpenSSL's BIO datapath requires a userspace pointer to encrypt into.
hardware: Netflix ~2016 100G NVMe flash appliance: Intel Xeon E5-2697A v4 @ 2.60GHz (16 core/32 HTT), 128GB DDR4-2400, 1x100GbE NIC (Chelsio T6), 4x NVMe
stars_or_usage: merged into FreeBSD 13 base system (r351522); used in production at Netflix
tradeoffs: FreeBSD/Linux kernel-specific (not portable to arbitrary C++ apps); NIC-offload path needs specific hardware (Chelsio T6, Mellanox ConnectX-6 DX); adds kernel attack surface for TLS handling; only covers the bulk-record encryption phase, handshake still uses userspace OpenSSL/rustls/etc.
caveats: The talk's only head-to-head numbers (68% vs 35% CPU at 90Gb/s) compare software kTLS to hardware-NIC kTLS, not directly to a measured plain-userspace-OpenSSL-with-sendfile baseline; the OpenSSL comparison is argued qualitatively (BIO datapath requires userspace copies) rather than benchmarked with a specific number on this slide deck. Capped at tier C for that reason.
